skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings. Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

4. //! Frame allocator — module-level singleton.
5. //!
6. //! The frame allocator is backed by a [`Bitmap`] and exposed as free functions over a
7. //! singleton so every in-kernel caller goes through the same state. No struct-valued handle is
8. //! passed around.
9. //!
10. //! Access to the frame allocator is synchronized externally and performed by a single thread, so
11. //! the backing bitmap uses non-atomic operations.

59. /// BSS-backed per-frame reference count storage. Indexed by frame number.
60. ///
61. /// Sits in BSS rather than on the kernel heap because the slab allocator caps single
62. /// allocations at a few hundred bytes, but a full refcount table for the configured
63. /// memory size is much larger.
64. ///
65. /// # Size impact
66. ///
67. /// This array is unconditionally reserved in BSS and scales linearly with the
68. /// configured machine memory size: `MEMORY_SIZE / FRAME_SIZE * size_of::<u8>()`
69. /// bytes (e.g. 256 KiB for a 1 GiB configuration). A `u8` is sufficient because at
70. /// most [`config::kernel::MAX_PROCESSES`] (≤ 255) processes can simultaneously share a
71. /// frame, so the refcount of any frame is bounded by 255.
72. ///
73. /// # Safety
74. ///
75. /// Accessed only through `Inner::refcount`, which is set up at boot from this storage
76. /// and never aliased. The kernel is single-threaded and runs with interrupts disabled,
77. /// so non-atomic access is sound.
78. static mut REFCOUNT_STORAGE: [u8; NFRAMES] = [0; NFRAMES];
79. 
80. /// Private state of the frame allocator singleton.
81. #[verus_verify]
82. struct Inner {
83.     /// A bitmap that keeps track of free/used frames.
84.     bitmap: Bitmap,
85.     /// Per-frame reference count. Indexed by frame number.
86.     ///
87.     /// Invariants:
88.     ///
89.     /// - `refcount.len() >= bitmap.number_of_bits()`.
90.     /// - `refcount[i] >= 1` iff bit `i` is set in `bitmap` (for `i < bitmap.number_of_bits()`).
91.     /// - `refcount[i] == 0` iff bit `i` is clear in `bitmap` (for `i < bitmap.number_of_bits()`).
92.     ///
93.     /// A refcount greater than one means that the frame is shared between multiple
94.     /// owners (e.g. parent and child after [`share`]). The frame is reclaimed (bitmap
95.     /// bit cleared) only when the refcount reaches zero.
96.     ///
97.     /// The element type is `u8`: the kernel caps the number of live processes at
98.     /// [`config::kernel::MAX_PROCESSES`] (≤ 255), so a frame can be shared by at most 255
99.     /// owners and the count always fits in a byte.
100.     refcount: &'static mut [u8],
101. }
102.

701. #[verus_spec(result =>
702.     ensures
703.         match result {
704.             Ok(_) => {
705.                 &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().initialized
706.                 &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.wf()
707.             },
708.             Err(_) => true,
709.         },
710. )]
711. pub(super) unsafe fn init(bitmap: Bitmap) -> Result<(), Error> {
712.     if unlikely(INSTANCE_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
713.         return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, "frame allocator already initialized"));
714.     }
715. 
716.     info!(
717.         "frame allocator: {} frames, {} MB",
718.         bitmap.number_of_bits(),
719.         (bitmap.number_of_bits() * mem::FRAME_SIZE) / constants::MEGABYTE,
720.     );
721. 
722.     let nframes: usize = bitmap.number_of_bits();
723.     if nframes > NFRAMES {
724.         return Err(Error::new(
725.             ErrorCode::InvalidArgument,
726.             "frame bitmap is larger than the configured refcount storage",
727.         ));
728.     }
729. 
730.     // SAFETY: single-threaded boot; no other reference to `REFCOUNT_STORAGE` exists.
731.     let refcount: &'static mut [u8] = unsafe { &mut REFCOUNT_STORAGE[..] };
732. 
733.     // Defensively sync refcounts with any bits already set in the incoming bitmap. The
734.     // current microvm boot path supplies an empty bitmap and performs all reservations
735.     // via `book()` / `alloc_range()` after `init()`, so this loop normally does nothing.
736.     // It is kept as a safety net so a future boot path that hands us a pre-populated
737.     // bitmap (for example to express firmware-reserved regions) does not silently end
738.     // up with `bitmap bit = 1, refcount = 0`, which would cause the first `free()` of
739.     // such a frame to be rejected as a spurious double-free.
740.     for (i, slot) in refcount.iter_mut().enumerate().take(nframes) {
741.         if matches!(bitmap.test(i), Ok(true)) {
742.             *slot = 1;
743.         }
744.     }
745. 
746.     // SAFETY: single-threaded boot; no other reference to `INSTANCE` exists.
747.     unsafe { INSTANCE.write(Inner { bitmap, refcount }) };
748.     INSTANCE_INIT.store(true, ORDER);
749.     Ok(())
750. }
751. 
752. /// Allocate a frame.
753. // Dependency contract for the manager layer: thin singleton wrapper around `Inner::alloc`.
754. // `external_body` until the `frame` free-function layer is verified; the manager bridges the
755. // returned address into its own abstract frame partition via a proof lemma.
756. #[verus_spec(result =>
757.     ensures
758.         match result {
759.             Ok(frame) => {
760.                 &&& frame.inv()
761.                 &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(frame@)
762.             },
763.             Err(_) => crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.free_frames.is_empty(),
764.         },
765. )]

770. /// # Description
771. ///
772. /// Allocates `count` physically contiguous frames.
773. ///
774. /// # Returns
775. ///
776. /// Returns the base `FrameAddress` of the contiguous range.
777. ///
778. // Dependency contract: thin singleton wrapper around `Inner::alloc_contiguous`. The base
779. // address is page-aligned on success. The address-space range bound (`base@ + count*PS <=
780. // usize::MAX`) is the fact the manager's per-frame index arithmetic relies upon; it follows
781. // from `Inner::alloc_contiguous`'s frame-set postcondition plus the allocator invariant
782. // (bridged in the proving phase).
783. #[verus_spec(result =>
784.     requires
785.         count > 0,
786.     ensures
787.         match result {
788.             Ok(base) => {
789.                 &&& base.inv()
790.                 &&& base@ + (count as int) * spec_page_size() <= usize::MAX as int
791.             },

793.         },
794. )]

800. /// # Description
801. ///
802. /// Returns the number of free frames in the system.
803. ///
804. /// # Returns
805. ///
806. /// The number of free frames in the system.
807. ///
808. // Dependency contract: reports the size of the free partition of the global frame allocator.
809. // The bitmap-level count (`number_of_bits - usage`) equals the abstract `free_count()`
810. // (`free_frames.len()`); this is bridged in the proving phase.
811. #[verus_spec(result =>
812.     ensures
813.         result as nat == crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.free_count(),

818. }

820. /// Free a frame previously returned by [`alloc`].
821. // Dependency contract: best-effort release of a frame. Callers (the manager's error-cleanup
822. // paths and the `Drop` impls) ignore the outcome, so no precondition is imposed and no abstract
823. // postcondition is promised. `opens_invariants none`/`no_unwind` so it is callable from
824. // `UserFrame::drop`/`KernelFrame::drop`. The underlying `Inner::free` precondition (`frame.inv()`)
825. // is discharged in the proving phase from the `FrameAddress` type invariant.
826. #[verus_spec(result =>
827.     ensures
828.         true,
829.     opens_invariants none
830.     no_unwind
831. )]
832. pub(super) fn free(frame: FrameAddress) -> Result<(), Error> {
833.     instance().free(frame)
834. }

836. ///
837. /// # Description
838. ///
839. /// Checks whether the frame allocator tracks the frame at the given physical address.
840. ///
841. /// # Returns
842. ///
843. /// Returns `true` when the frame allocator tracks the frame at `phys_addr`.
844. ///
845. // Dependency contract: pure coverage query over the global frame partition. `true` iff the
846. // allocator tracks the frame (allocated or free), i.e. `phys_view().frames.covers(phys_addr@)`.
847. // Used by the MMIO boot path to skip frames above RAM that the bitmap does not cover.
848. #[verus_spec(ret =>
849.     requires
850.         phys_addr.inv(),
851.     ensures
852.         ret <==> crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.covers(phys_addr@),
853. )]
854. pub(super) fn is_covered(phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>) -> bool {
855.     instance().is_covered(phys_addr)
856. }

858. /// Reserve a frame so [`alloc`] will skip it.
859. // Dependency contract: singleton wrapper around `Inner::book`. Reserves a covered, previously
860. // free frame (refcount becomes 1) so `alloc` never hands it out. The per-frame reservation is
861. // recorded in the global partition; the booking transition lives in `Inner::book` and is bridged
862. // to `phys_view().frames` in the proving phase. The boot caller (`book_mmio_regions`) re-derives
863. // the region-level booking facts via its own lemmas.
864. #[verus_spec(result =>
865.     requires
866.         phys_addr.inv(),
867.     ensures
868.         match result {
869.             Ok(()) => crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.reserved(phys_addr@),
870.             Err(_) => !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.free_frames.contains(phys_addr@),
871.         },
872. )]
873. pub(super) fn book(phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>) -> Result<(), Error> {
874.     instance().book(phys_addr)
875. }
876. 
877. /// Book every frame in the given physical memory region.
878. // Dependency contract: singleton wrapper around `Inner::alloc_range`. On success every frame in
879. // the region (which must all be free) is reserved with refcount 1. The region-level transition
880. // lives in `Inner::alloc_range`; the boot caller (`book_physical_memory_regions`) re-derives the
881. // region-set booking facts via its own lemmas.
882. #[verus_spec(result =>
883.     requires
884.         region.inv(),
885.     ensures
886.         match result {
887.             Ok(()) => crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.all_reserved(
888.                 crate::mm::phys::region_frame_addrs(region@.start, region@.size)),
889.             Err(_) => !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.all_free(
890.                 crate::mm::phys::region_frame_addrs(region@.start, region@.size)),
891.         },
892. )]
893. pub(super) fn alloc_range(region: &TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>) -> Result<(), Error> {
894.     instance().alloc_range(region)
895. }
896. 
897. /// Add a new reference to an already-allocated frame (e.g. for copy-on-write sharing).
898. // Dependency contract: singleton wrapper around `Inner::share`. On success the frame is (still)
899. // allocated; the per-frame reference-count increment lives in the global partition and is pinned
900. // to `phys_view().frames` in the proving phase. `external_body` until the free-function layer is
901. // verified.
902. #[verus_spec(result =>
903.     requires
904.         frame.inv(),
905.     ensures
906.         match result {
907.             Ok(()) => crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(frame@),
908.             Err(_) => !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(frame@)
909.                 || crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.refcounts[frame@] >= 255,
910.         },
911. )]
912. pub(super) fn share(frame: FrameAddress) -> Result<(), Error> {
913.     instance().share(frame)
914. }
915. 
916. /// Returns the current reference count of an already-allocated frame.

---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
   strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
   functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
   (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
   record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
   the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
   `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
  in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
- **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
  cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
  `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |

## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost

- **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
- **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.

See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.

## Warnings

Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:

- **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
  the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
  choose triggers automatically.
- **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
  to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.

## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)

Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
`axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.

**Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax

```rust
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

---
name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. See `verus-syntax` for attribute-based syntax
reference. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function,
   following the order from the `verification-order` skill if a
   verification plan exists. Do not move to the next function until the
   current one verifies cleanly.
   
   The current module's functions must NOT have `external_body`.
   Do NOT add `external_body` to any function during proving.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Never weaken specs.** If a spec is hard to prove, the proof strategy
   is wrong — not the spec. Do not relax `requires`, weaken `ensures`,
   or remove clauses to make proofs easier. The spec is the contract.

4. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

5. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
   Trigger warnings are especially common and must not be left: add
   explicit `#[trigger]` annotations or restructure quantifiers until
   all trigger warnings are gone.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`,
  cfg-gated exec code; all must be resolved in current module.
  `external_body` on direct callees in dependency modules is expected
  until those modules are verified; **Never** mark callers
  (upstream modules) as `external_body`
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

---

## Proof Organization

- **Write proof helpers in `.proof.rs` from the start.** If a proof block
  would exceed ~5 lines, don't write it inline — define a `proof fn` in the
  `.proof.rs` file and call it from the inline `proof { }` block. Same for
  loop invariants with more than ~5 clauses: define a `spec fn` predicate in
  `.proof.rs` and reference it in the `invariant` clause. This avoids
  cluttering exec code and eliminates extraction work later.
- Keep proof fn granular: one lemma per function, chain via `assert ... by { lemma_call(); }`
- Default: make specs `opaque`, only `reveal()` where needed

## Inductive Invariants

Functions with loops or recursion need inductive invariants — without them
Verus cannot verify the function. If loop invariants already exist, review
them before attempting the proof. When `admit()` is removed, existing
invariants may turn out to be too weak. Strengthen them — do not work
around the failure with cheating. If no invariant exists yet, define one
before attempting the proof.

1. **Review the existing invariant.** Read the `invariant` clause (or the
   `spec fn` it references). Understand what it claims and what it misses.
2. **Strengthen as needed.** Add missing clauses or tighten existing ones
   based on Verus error messages. Getting the invariant right on the first
   try is rare — iterate until it passes. Never bypass a failing obligation
   with `admit`, `assume`, or `external_body`.
3. **Verify the three obligations:**
   - **Base case** — the invariant holds on entry (before the first
     iteration, or for the base constructor).
   - **Inductive step** — if the invariant holds before an iteration /
     recursive call, it holds after.
   - **Sufficiency** — the invariant, combined with the loop exit
     condition, implies the postcondition.

name: verification-order
description: "Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work."
---

# Verification Order

## Purpose

When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
already proven when you reach it.

## How to Get the Order

A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:

```
{logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
```

If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:

```bash
# Show function order for a specific module
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"

# Glob pattern to match multiple modules
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "bitmap::*"
```

If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).

## How to Use the Order

1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
   The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
   may call earlier ones.
3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
   to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
   rule but with a concrete ordering.
4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
   modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
   an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.

## Output Format

```
## kernel::mm::phys::kpool
   crate: kernel  |  file: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kpool.rs

    #  Function                        Line  In-module deps
  ───  ──────────────────────────────  ─────  ──────────────────────────────
    1  KpoolInner::alloc               L56   —
    2  KernelFrame::deref_mut          L160  —
    3  KernelFrame::clear              L144  KernelFrame::deref_mut
    4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
```

Use `-v` to also see cross-module dependency modules.

Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.

name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. See `verus-syntax` for attribute-based syntax
reference. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function,
   following the order from the `verification-order` skill if a
   verification plan exists. Do not move to the next function until the
   current one verifies cleanly.
   
   The current module's functions must NOT have `external_body`.
   Do NOT add `external_body` to any function during proving.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Never weaken specs.** If a spec is hard to prove, the proof strategy
   is wrong — not the spec. Do not relax `requires`, weaken `ensures`,
   or remove clauses to make proofs easier. The spec is the contract.

4. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

5. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
   Trigger warnings are especially common and must not be left: add
   explicit `#[trigger]` annotations or restructure quantifiers until
   all trigger warnings are gone.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`,
  cfg-gated exec code; all must be resolved in current module.
  `external_body` on direct callees in dependency modules is expected
  until those modules are verified; **Never** mark callers
  (upstream modules) as `external_body`
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

---

## Proof Organization

- **Write proof helpers in `.proof.rs` from the start.** If a proof block
  would exceed ~5 lines, don't write it inline — define a `proof fn` in the
  `.proof.rs` file and call it from the inline `proof { }` block. Same for
  loop invariants with more than ~5 clauses: define a `spec fn` predicate in
  `.proof.rs` and reference it in the `invariant` clause. This avoids
  cluttering exec code and eliminates extraction work later.
- Keep proof fn granular: one lemma per function, chain via `assert ... by { lemma_call(); }`
- Default: make specs `opaque`, only `reveal()` where needed

## Inductive Invariants

Functions with loops or recursion need inductive invariants — without them
Verus cannot verify the function. If loop invariants already exist, review
them before attempting the proof. When `admit()` is removed, existing
invariants may turn out to be too weak. Strengthen them — do not work
around the failure with cheating. If no invariant exists yet, define one
before attempting the proof.

1. **Review the existing invariant.** Read the `invariant` clause (or the
   `spec fn` it references). Understand what it claims and what it misses.
2. **Strengthen as needed.** Add missing clauses or tighten existing ones
   based on Verus error messages. Getting the invariant right on the first
   try is rare — iterate until it passes. Never bypass a failing obligation
   with `admit`, `assume`, or `external_body`.
3. **Verify the three obligations:**
   - **Base case** — the invariant holds on entry (before the first
     iteration, or for the base constructor).
   - **Inductive step** — if the invariant holds before an iteration /
     recursive call, it holds after.
   - **Sufficiency** — the invariant, combined with the loop exit
     condition, implies the postcondition.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. // PhysMemoryManager - Specifications
5. //
6. // This file contains specification functions and view types.
7. 
8. verus! {
9. 
10. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
11. use vstd::map::*;
12. 
13. pub uninterp spec fn byte_at_address(ptr: int) -> u8;
14. 
15. /// Abstract view of the frame allocator (`frame::Inner`).
16. ///
17. /// Captures which physical frames are currently allocated vs. free,
18. /// together with a per-frame reference count that models shared
19. /// ownership (e.g. copy-on-write after `share()`).
20. pub struct FrameAllocView
21. {
22.     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
23.     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
24.     /// Maps each allocated frame address to its reference count.
25.     /// A frame is present in the map iff it is currently allocated.
26.     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
27. }
28. 
29. impl FrameAllocView
30. {
31.     pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool
32.     {
33.         // Page-alignment
34.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
35.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
36.         // Disjoint
37.         &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
38.         // Allocated ↔ refcount consistency: a frame is allocated iff it has a positive refcount
39.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) <==>
40.             self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) && self.refcounts[addr] > 0
41.         // Free frames have no refcount entry
42.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==>
43.             !self.refcounts.contains_key(addr)
44.         // Refcount bounded by u8 range
45.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) ==>
46.             0 < self.refcounts[addr] <= 255
47.     }
48. }
49. 
50. //==================================================================================================
51. // LinkedList — external type registration
52. //==================================================================================================
53. //
54. // `vstd` provides no specification for `alloc::collections::LinkedList`, so it must be
55. // registered as an external type before it can appear in spec signatures. Only the type
56. // is registered here; no `View`/iterator specification is provided, because the orphan
57. // rule forbids a downstream crate from implementing vstd's `View` / `ForLoopGhostIterator`
58. // traits for the foreign `LinkedList` / `linked_list::Iter` types. As a consequence, the
59. // two helpers that iterate a `LinkedList` in a `for` loop (`book_physical_memory_regions`,
60. // `book_mmio_regions`) cannot have their bodies verified and are `external_body`. See
61. // `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-mod/bugs.md`.
62. 
63. use ::core::alloc::Allocator;
64. 
65. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
66. #[verifier::external_body]
67. #[verifier::accept_recursive_types(T)]
68. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
69. pub struct ExLinkedList<T, A: Allocator>(::alloc::collections::LinkedList<T, A>);
70. 
71. //==================================================================================================
72. // Physical-memory subsystem view
73. //==================================================================================================
74. 
75. /// Abstract view of the global physical-memory subsystem managed by `mm::phys`.
76. ///
77. /// Pure ghost description — names no `MaybeUninit`, `AtomicBool`, bitmap, refcount slice,
78. /// or any other storage mechanism. It wraps the existing frame-allocator view
79. /// (`FrameAllocView`) with the two liveness facts the caller depends on.
80. pub ghost struct PhysModView {
81.     /// The frame allocator singleton has been initialized (`frame::init` ran
82.     /// successfully). All `frames`-related guarantees are meaningful only when this holds.
83.     pub initialized: bool,
84.     /// Abstract frame-allocator state: which physical frames are allocated (reserved) vs.
85.     /// free, with per-frame refcounts. This is the existing `FrameAllocView`.
86.     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
87.     /// The `PhysMemoryManager` singleton has been initialized with a fresh user page pool.
88.     pub manager_ready: bool,
89. }
90. 
91. /// Current abstract state of the global physical-memory subsystem.
92. ///
93. /// Uninterpreted accessor: the subsystem state lives in module-level singletons
94. /// (`frame::INSTANCE`/`INSTANCE_INIT` and the `PhysMemoryManager`/`Upool` singletons)
95. /// whose value is not directly spec-readable. The cross-call transition (`v -> v'`) is
96. /// realized in the proving phase by a ghost token over those singletons (see
97. /// `view_design.md` section 8); during the specification phase it is read like `self@`.
98. pub uninterp spec fn phys_view() -> PhysModView;
99. 
100. impl PhysModView {
101.     /// Well-formedness invariant of the subsystem.
102.     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
103.         // Once the allocator is up, the frame partition is well formed.
104.         &&& self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
105.         // The manager layer can only be up if the allocator is up.
106.         &&& self.manager_ready ==> self.initialized
107.     }
108. 
109.     /// The subsystem is fully brought up and self-consistent.
110.     pub open spec fn live(self) -> bool {
111.         &&& self.initialized
112.         &&& self.manager_ready
113.         &&& self.frames.wf()
114.     }
115. }
116. 
117. //==================================================================================================
118. // Frame-set vocabulary (on the existing FrameAllocView)
119. //==================================================================================================
120. 
121. impl FrameAllocView {
122.     /// The allocator tracks (covers) the frame at `addr` — it is one of the frames this
123.     /// allocator knows about, allocated or free. Models `frame::is_covered`.
124.     pub open spec fn covers(self, addr: int) -> bool {
125.         self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) || self.free_frames.contains(addr)
126.     }
127. 
128.     /// The frame at `addr` is reserved: present in the allocated set, hence `alloc()` can
129.     /// never return it. This is the core caller-visible fact a "booked" frame satisfies.
130.     pub open spec fn reserved(self, addr: int) -> bool {
131.         self.allocated_frames.contains(addr)
132.     }
133. 
134.     /// Every frame address in `set` is reserved.
135.     pub open spec fn all_reserved(self, set: Set<int>) -> bool {
136.         forall|a: int| set.contains(a) ==> self.reserved(a)
137.     }
138. 
139.     /// Every frame address in `set` is currently free (booking precondition: a range can be
140.     /// booked only if it is entirely free).
141.     pub open spec fn all_free(self, set: Set<int>) -> bool {
142.         forall|a: int| #[trigger] set.contains(a) ==> self.free_frames.contains(a)
143.     }
144. 
145.     /// Reserve every frame in `set` (each assumed free in `self`): move it from
146.     /// `free_frames` to `allocated_frames` with refcount 1.
147.     pub open spec fn book_all(self, set: Set<int>) -> FrameAllocView {
148.         FrameAllocView {
149.             allocated_frames: self.allocated_frames.union(set),
150.             free_frames: self.free_frames.difference(set),
151.             refcounts: self.refcounts.union_prefer_right(
152.                 Map::new(|a: int| set.contains(a), |a: int| 1int),
153.             ),
154.         }
155.     }
156. 
157.     /// Reserve only the *covered* frames of `set`; skip the rest (coverage-gated). Models
158.     /// the MMIO booking rule.
159.     pub open spec fn book_covered(self, set: Set<int>) -> FrameAllocView {
160.         self.book_all(set.filter(|a: int| self.covers(a)))
161.     }
162. }
163. 
164. /// Page-aligned physical frame addresses covered by a region `[start, start + size)`.
165. /// Mirrors the frame-set computation used by `frame::alloc_range`.
166. pub open spec fn region_frame_addrs(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
167.     let start_frame_number = start / spec_page_size();
168.     let end_frame_number = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
169.     vstd::set_lib::set_int_range(start_frame_number, end_frame_number)
170.         .map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
171. }
172. 
173. /// The set of physical frame addresses covered by all regions in a physical
174. /// non-usable-memory list. Uninterpreted: `LinkedList` has no Verus model, so its contents
175. /// cannot be folded over in spec; this names the abstract union of `region_frame_addrs`
176. /// over the list, which is all the contract needs.
177. pub uninterp spec fn phys_regions_frame_set(
178.     regions: &::alloc::collections::LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>>,
179. ) -> Set<int>;
180. 
181. /// The set of physical frame addresses covered by all MMIO regions in a list (after
182. /// GVA->GPA translation). Uninterpreted for the same reason as `phys_regions_frame_set`.
183. pub uninterp spec fn mmio_regions_frame_set(
184.     regions: &::alloc::collections::LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<VirtualAddress>>,
185. ) -> Set<int>;
186. 
187. } // end verus!
188.

3. 
4. //==================================================================================================
5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================
7. 
8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("number.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("number.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use crate::mem;
15. 
16. //==================================================================================================
17. // Structures
18. //==================================================================================================
19. 
20. ///
21. /// # Description
22. ///
23. /// A type that represents a frame number.
24. /// A frame number is in the range from `0` to [`Self::MAX`] (inclusive).
25. ///
26. #[verus_verify]
27. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
28. pub struct FrameNumber(usize);
29. 
30. //==================================================================================================
31. // Implementations
32. //==================================================================================================
33. 
34. #[verus_verify]
35. impl FrameNumber {
36.     /// The maximum frame number.
37.     pub const MAX: usize = mem::MAX_ADDRESS / mem::FRAME_SIZE - 1;
38. 
39.     #[verus_spec(ensures Self::NULL@ == 0)]
40.     pub const NULL: Self = Self(0);
41. 
42.     ///
43.     /// # Description
44.     ///
45.     /// Constructs a [`FrameNumber`].
46.     ///
47.     /// # Parameters
48.     ///
49.     /// - `value`: The value of the frame number.
50.     ///
51.     /// # Returns
52.     ///
53.     /// - `Some(`[`FrameNumber`]`)`: Upon success.
54.     /// - `None`: If the value is greater than [`Self::MAX`].
55.     ///
56.     #[verus_spec(result =>
57.         ensures
58.             value as int <= Self::spec_max() ==> (result is Some
59.                 && (result->Some_0)@ == value as int),
60.             value as int > Self::spec_max() ==> result is None,
61.     )]
62.     pub fn from_raw_value(value: usize) -> Option<Self> {
63.         if value > Self::MAX {
64.             return None;
65.         }
66. 
67.         Some(Self(value))
68.     }
69. 
70.     ///
71.     /// # Description
72.     ///
73.     /// Converts a [`FrameNumber`] into a raw value.
74.     ///
75.     /// # Returns
76.     ///
77.     /// The raw value of the target [`FrameNumber`].
78.     ///
79.     #[verus_spec(result =>
80.         ensures
81.             result as int == self@,
82.             0 <= self@ <= Self::spec_max(),
83.     )]
84.     pub fn into_raw_value(self) -> usize {
85.         proof! { use_type_invariant(self); }
86.         self.0
87.     }
88. }
89.

92. //==================================================================================================

94. /// Tests if [`FrameNumber::from_raw_value()`] successfully constructs frame zero.
95. #[test]
96. fn test_frame_number_from_raw_value_zero() {
97.     let raw_value: usize = 0;
98.     let frame_number: FrameNumber = FrameNumber::from_raw_value(raw_value).unwrap();
99.     assert_eq!(frame_number.into_raw_value(), raw_value);
100. }
101.

103. #[test]

description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

# Frame allocator Verus proof plan

## Target: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs — 8 Inner methods + free-fn wrappers

## Central finding (resolved)
`into_frame_number()` (address layer, now properly verified) requires the
frame-number bound `spec_frame_number(addr@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`.
The 6 address-consuming Inner methods only have alignment (`inv()`), so the
bound is NOT derivable for the single top-of-space aligned address
`usize::MAX-4095` (frame `usize::MAX/4096`, which arch deliberately excludes
via `FrameNumber::MAX = MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE - 1` to avoid end-addr overflow).
=> `into_frame_number().unwrap()` PANICS on that aligned input — a latent
panic-on-valid-input bug. Every such method already has a downstream guard
(`>= refcount.len()`, `>= num_bits`, or bitmap `Err`) that rejects oversized
frame numbers gracefully; the panic just fires first.

### Fix (auto-fixable: unchecked conversion / missing-guard)
Replace `X.into_frame_number().into_raw_value()` with the total equivalent
`X.into_raw_value() / mem::FRAME_SIZE` (same value `addr@/PAGE_SIZE`, no panic).
Record in bugs.md. No spec weakening; no arch/address changes.

## Method order (leaves first)
1. is_covered  (read-only; into_raw_value/FRAME_SIZE + num_bits compare)
2. refcount    (read-only; refcount.len guard)
3. share       (mut refcount only)
4. free        (mut refcount + bitmap.clear)
5. book        (bitmap.set + refcount)
6. alloc       (bitmap.alloc + FrameNumber::from_raw_value)  -- already total
7. alloc_contiguous (bitmap.alloc_range)                     -- already total
8. alloc_range (two loops; needs loop invariants)

## Wrappers (free fns): mutating ones (alloc, alloc_contiguous, free, book,
alloc_range, free_count) are TCB external_body (post-mutation phys_view()
unprovable). is_covered/share/refcount proven in-body if they pass.

## Status

- [ ] source fix (6 methods)
- [ ] bug record
- [ ] remove stray lemma_bound_test
- [ ] proofs

## [auto-fixed] panic-on-valid-input: `into_frame_number().unwrap()` on top-of-space aligned address

**Where**: `Inner::free` (frame.rs:300), `Inner::share` (:381), `Inner::refcount` (:444),
`Inner::book` (:499), `Inner::is_covered` (:536), `Inner::alloc_range` (:587).

**What**: Each method converted an input address to a frame index via
`X.into_frame_number().into_raw_value()`. `PhysicalAddress/FrameAddress::into_frame_number`
is a *checked* conversion: internally `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(addr >> FRAME_SHIFT).unwrap()`,
which **panics** when the frame number exceeds `FrameNumber::MAX = MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE - 1`.

**Why**: With `MAX_ADDRESS == usize::MAX`, the single page-aligned address
`usize::MAX - 4095` maps to frame `usize::MAX/4096 = FrameNumber::MAX + 1`, which arch
deliberately excludes (the top frame's end address `base + FRAME_SIZE` would overflow `usize`).
The method preconditions only guarantee page-alignment (`frame.inv()` / `phys_addr.inv()`),
which does **not** rule out this address. So a caller passing the top-of-space aligned address
crashes the kernel. Each method already has a downstream guard that rejects oversized frame
numbers gracefully (`frame_number >= self.refcount.len()`, `>= num_bits`, or bitmap `Err`),
but the panic in `into_frame_number` fires *before* the guard, making the guard unreachable
for that input.

**Verification Failure**: `into_frame_number` requires
`spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`; unprovable from page-alignment alone
(false for `self@ == usize::MAX - 4095`). Command: `make verify-kernel MODULE=mm::phys`.

**How Verus Helped**: The panic is unreachable on real hardware (physical addresses never reach
the top of the 64-bit space), so neither testing nor review would surface it. Formal
verification, modeling `MAX_ADDRESS == usize::MAX`, exposed the reachable `unwrap` panic.

**Severity**: safety-critical (kernel panic / DoS on a precondition-satisfying input).

**Suggested/Applied Fix**: Replace the checked, panicking conversion with the equivalent
*total* computation `X.into_raw_value() / mem::FRAME_SIZE` (same value `addr@ / PAGE_SIZE` for
all in-range frames). The existing downstream guards then reject the out-of-range top frame
cleanly with `Err`/`false`, matching each method's `Err`/coverage postcondition.

**Auto-Fixed**: Yes — replaced `X.into_frame_number().into_raw_value()` with
`X.into_raw_value() / mem::FRAME_SIZE` at the six sites above (`// VERUS BUG FIX:` comments).
No specs weakened; no changes to the arch/address layers.
EOF

arguments.prompt:
You are completing Verus proofs for the Nanvix kernel frame allocator. The analysis and setup are DONE; your job is to write the proof bodies and helper lemmas until verification passes with 0 errors, 0 `admit()`, 0 `assume()`.

# Repository
/home/ruize/nanvix-phy-specs

# Target file
src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs  (with includes frame.spec.rs and frame.proof.rs)

# Verify command (run from repo root)
`make verify-kernel MODULE=mm::phys`
This compiles the whole kernel crate and is SLOW (~4-7 min). Use: `timeout 600 make verify-kernel MODULE=mm::phys 2>&1 | tail -80` and run with bash initial_wait of 400+, reading more with read_bash. Do NOT abandon a run early.

# What is ALREADY done (DO NOT undo)
1. `instance()`, `init()` and the 8 free-function wrappers (`alloc`, `alloc_contiguous`, `free_count`, `free`, `book`, `alloc_range`, `share`, `refcount`) already have `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` — these are TCB-allowed (see verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md). LEAVE THEM. The `is_covered` free-fn wrapper is NOT external_body and must be proven in-body.
2. A latent panic bug was fixed: the 6 address-consuming Inner methods (free, share, refcount, book, is_covered, alloc_range) now compute the frame index via `X.into_raw_value() / mem::FRAME_SIZE` instead of `X.into_frame_number().into_raw_value()` (which panics on the top-of-space aligned address). These `// VERUS BUG FIX:` lines are CORRECT — keep them. Recorded in verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-frame/bugs.md.

# YOUR TASK: prove these 8 Inner methods (remove the 3 remaining `admit()` at the tops of alloc, alloc_contiguous, alloc_range; the other 5 already have admit removed and need proof bodies/assertions to verify):
- `Inner::is_covered` (read-only)
- `Inner::refcount` (read-only)
- `Inner::share` (mutates refcount vec)
- `Inner::free` (mutates refcount vec + bitmap.clear)
- `Inner::book` (bitmap.set + refcount vec)
- `Inner::alloc` (bitmap.alloc + FrameNumber::from_raw_value + FrameAddress::from_frame_number)
- `Inner::alloc_contiguous` (bitmap.alloc_range + loop)
- `Inner::alloc_range` (two `for` loops over start..=end; currently `verus_spec(invariant false)` placeholders — replace with real loop invariants)
Also prove the `is_covered` free-function wrapper (instance().is_covered + covers() relation).

# HARD RULES (violating these fails the task)
- Do NOT weaken/modify/delete/rename any `requires`/`ensures` on any function, nor the `#[verus_spec]` on the Inner methods or wrappers.
- Do NOT modify these definitions: `Inner::inv` (frame.spec.rs), and in frame.proof.rs: `frame_addr_of`, `View for Inner` (the `view()`), `Inner::internal_inv`. You MAY ADD new helper `proof fn` lemmas and `spec fn` helpers to frame.proof.rs.
- Do NOT add `external_body` to anything new. Do NOT add `assume()` or leave `admit()`.
- Do NOT touch other modules' specs.

# KEY FACTS (already verified by reading the code) — use these
## View (frame.proof.rs, DO NOT MODIFY):
- `Inner@.allocated_frames = { frame_addr_of(i) : self.bitmap@.set_bits.contains(i) }` (trigger: set_bits.contains(i))
- `Inner@.free_frames = { frame_addr_of(i) : 0<=i<num_bits && !set_bits.contains(i) }`
- `Inner@.refcounts = Map::new(key: exists i set_bits.contains(i) && addr==frame_addr_of(i), val: self.refcount@[addr/PS] as int)`
- `frame_addr_of(i) = i * spec_page_size()`  ; `spec_page_size() = arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE as int = 4096`
## Inner::internal_inv (closed; available under self.inv()):
- `self.bitmap.inv()`, `spec_page_size() > 0`
- `self.refcount@.len() >= self.bitmap@.num_bits`
- `forall i in [0,num_bits): set_bits.contains(i) <==> refcount@[i] > 0`
- `forall i in [0,num_bits): !set_bits.contains(i) <==> refcount@[i] == 0`
- `forall i in [0,num_bits) with set_bits.contains(i): 0 < refcount@[i] <= 255`
- `forall i in [0,num_bits): 0 <= frame_addr_of(i) <= usize::MAX`
- `forall i in [num_bits, refcount@.len()): refcount@[i] == 0`
## Inner::inv() = self@.wf() && self.internal_inv(). FrameAllocView::wf is in src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.spec.rs — READ IT to know what wf requires (you must re-establish it in `final(self)@.wf()`).
## Bitmap (src/libs/bitmap/src/lib.rs + lib.spec.rs) — all total, full ensures:
- `inv()` guarantees `0 < num_bits < u32::MAX`, `usage()==set_bits.len()<=num_bits`, set_bits.wf (all in [0,num_bits)), set_bits.finite.
- `is_bit_set(i) <==> set_bits.contains(i)` (open spec).
- `number_of_bits()`: requires inv; ensures `result as int==num_bits, result>0, result<u32::MAX`.
- `usage()`: ensures `result as int==usage()<=num_bits`.
- `alloc()`: Ok(index): `0<=index<num_bits`, `set_bits==old.set_bits.insert(index)`, `!old.is_bit_set(index)`, `is_bit_set(index)`, usage+1, num_bits unchanged. Err: old.is_full(), unchanged.
- `alloc_range(size)`: requires `0<size<=num_bits`. Ok(start): `0<=start`, `start+size<=num_bits`, `set_bits==old.set_bits.union(range_set(start,start+size))`, old all_bits_unset_in_range(start,start+size), num_bits unchanged. Err: unchanged.
- `set(index)`: Ok: `index<num_bits`, `set_bits==old.set_bits.insert(index)`, `!old.is_bit_set(index)`, num_bits unchanged. Err: `index>=num_bits || old.is_bit_set(index)`, unchanged.
- `clear(index)`: Ok: `index<num_bits`, `set_bits==old.set_bits.remove(index)`, num_bits unchanged. Err: `index>=num_bits || !old.is_bit_set(index)`, unchanged.
- `test(index)`: Ok(b): `index<num_bits`, `b==is_bit_set(index)`. Err: `index>=num_bits`.
- `range_set(a,b) = set_int_range(a,b)` ; `all_bits_unset_in_range(a,b) = forall i in [a,b): !set_bits.contains(i)`.
## Address helpers (available specs):
- `FrameAddress::into_raw_value(self) -> usize` ensures `result as int == self@`.
- `<PageAligned<T> as Address>::into_raw_value(a) -> usize` ensures `result as int == a@` (frame.spec.rs assume_spec).
- `FrameAddress::inv() = self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (alignment). Same for PageAligned::inv.
- `FrameAddress::from_frame_number(fnum)`: ensures `Ok`, `(Ok_0).inv()`, `(Ok_0)@ == spec_from_number(spec_frame_raw_value(fnum)) == fnum@ * spec_page_size()`.
- `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(v) -> Option`: ensures `v<=spec_max() ==> Some && Some_0@==v`; `v>spec_max() ==> None`. `spec_max() = (usize::MAX/4096 - 1) as nat ~ 4.5e15`.
- `FrameNumber::into_raw_value()` ensures `result as int==self@` and `0<=self@<=spec_max()`.
- Since `num_bits < u32::MAX < spec_max()`, any bitmap index `< num_bits` satisfies `<= spec_max()`, so `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(index)` returns `Some` in alloc/alloc_contiguous.
## region (alloc_range): `region: &TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>`. READ src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/region.rs for `region.start()` (returns FrameAddress? or PageAligned), `region.size()`, `region@`, `region.inv()`. The spec uses `region@.start`, `region@.size`. The bugs.md notes a possible off-by-one between the inclusive `start..=end` loop and the half-open spec range; resolve it using region.inv() facts (e.g. start & size page-aligned). If region.inv() does NOT guarantee size%PS==0, the body's `start + size/FS - 1` vs spec `(start+size)/PS` must be reconciled — investigate region.inv() carefully before concluding.

# PROOF STRATEGY GUIDANCE
Add helper lemmas to frame.proof.rs such as:
- `lemma_aligned_addr_index(a)`: requires `a % spec_page_size()==0`, `spec_page_size()>0`; ensures `frame_addr_of(a / spec_page_size()) == a`. Proof via `vstd::arithmetic::div_mod::lemma_fundamental_div_mod(a, spec_page_size())`.
- `lemma_frame_addr_injective(i, j)`: from `frame_addr_of(i)==frame_addr_of(j)` and PS>0 derive `i==j` (use `vstd::arithmetic::mul::lemma_mul_is_commutative` + division, e.g. `(i*PS)/PS==i` via `lemma_div_multiples_vanish`).
- A lemma: for `fnum` with `frame_addr_of(fnum)==addr`, `self@.allocated_frames.contains(addr) <==> self.bitmap@.set_bits.contains(fnum)` (forward: witness; backward: injectivity). Similarly for free_frames using `0<=fnum<num_bits`.
- Lemmas relating the updated bitmap.set_bits (insert/remove/union) and updated refcount vec to the new `Inner@` sets/map — these are the crux for free/book/share/alloc/alloc_contiguous/alloc_range. Use `Set`/`Map` extensionality (`assert_sets_equal!`, `assert_maps_equal!` from vstd) to prove `final(self)@ == FrameAllocView{...}`.
For mutating methods, note the View is recomputed from the FINAL bitmap.set_bits and refcount vec; prove each field equals the spec'd insert/remove/union. Re-establish `final(self)@.wf()` and `internal_inv()`.
For `share`/`free`/`refcount`, the index comes from the input address; after `frame_number = frame.into_raw_value()/FRAME_SIZE`, establish `frame_addr_of(frame_number) == frame@` via the alignment lemma. The downstream `>= refcount.len()` guards map to the `Err` postconditions (frame not in allocated_frames) — prove via injectivity that an oversized index's address is not in the set.

# WORKFLOW
1. Run baseline `make verify-kernel MODULE=mm::phys` to see current errors.
2. Prove methods in this order (easiest first), re-running after each: is_covered, refcount, share, free, book, alloc, alloc_contiguous, alloc_range. Then the is_covered wrapper.
3. Iterate until 0 errors. Then verify NO admit/assume remain: `grep -n "admit()\|assume(" src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.proof.rs`.
4. Finally run `make verify` (whole workspace) to confirm no regressions. Report the final make verify-kernel and make verify result counts.

# IMPORTANT
- If a method seems genuinely unprovable, re-read its spec and the View/internal_inv carefully before concluding — almost certainly it needs more assertions/lemmas, not a spec change. Never weaken a spec.
- Keep proof code clean. Prefer `assert(...) by { ... }`, `assert_sets_equal!`, `assert_maps_equal!`, and small reusable lemmas.
- Report progress concisely and the final verification status (errors, admit count, assume count) when done.

18. /// together with a per-frame reference count that models shared
19. /// ownership (e.g. copy-on-write after `share()`).
20. pub struct FrameAllocView
21. {
22.     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
23.     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
24.     /// Maps each allocated frame address to its reference count.
25.     /// A frame is present in the map iff it is currently allocated.
26.     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
27. }
28. 
29. impl FrameAllocView
30. {
31.     pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool
32.     {
33.         // Page-alignment
34.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
35.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
36.         // Disjoint
37.         &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
38.         // Allocated ↔ refcount consistency: a frame is allocated iff it has a positive refcount
39.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) <==>
40.             self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) && self.refcounts[addr] > 0
41.         // Free frames have no refcount entry
42.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==>
43.             !self.refcounts.contains_key(addr)
44.         // Refcount bounded by u8 range
45.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) ==>
46.             0 < self.refcounts[addr] <= 255
47.     }
48. }
49.

51. // LinkedList — external type registration
52. //==================================================================================================
53. //
54. // `vstd` provides no specification for `alloc::collections::LinkedList`, so it must be
55. // registered as an external type before it can appear in spec signatures. Only the type
56. // is registered here; no `View`/iterator specification is provided, because the orphan
57. // rule forbids a downstream crate from implementing vstd's `View` / `ForLoopGhostIterator`
58. // traits for the foreign `LinkedList` / `linked_list::Iter` types. As a consequence, the
59. // two helpers that iterate a `LinkedList` in a `for` loop (`book_physical_memory_regions`,
60. // `book_mmio_regions`) cannot have their bodies verified and are `external_body`. See
61. // `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-mod/bugs.md`.

66. #[verifier::external_body]
67. #[verifier::accept_recursive_types(T)]
68. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
69. pub struct ExLinkedList<T, A: Allocator>(::alloc::collections::LinkedList<T, A>);

72. // Physical-memory subsystem view
73. //==================================================================================================
74. 
75. /// Abstract view of the global physical-memory subsystem managed by `mm::phys`.
76. ///
77. /// Pure ghost description — names no `MaybeUninit`, `AtomicBool`, bitmap, refcount slice,
78. /// or any other storage mechanism. It wraps the existing frame-allocator view
79. /// (`FrameAllocView`) with the two liveness facts the caller depends on.
80. pub ghost struct PhysModView {
81.     /// The frame allocator singleton has been initialized (`frame::init` ran
82.     /// successfully). All `frames`-related guarantees are meaningful only when this holds.
83.     pub initialized: bool,
84.     /// Abstract frame-allocator state: which physical frames are allocated (reserved) vs.
85.     /// free, with per-frame refcounts. This is the existing `FrameAllocView`.
86.     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
87.     /// The `PhysMemoryManager` singleton has been initialized with a fresh user page pool.
88.     pub manager_ready: bool,
89. }
90. 
91. /// Current abstract state of the global physical-memory subsystem.
92. ///
93. /// Uninterpreted accessor: the subsystem state lives in module-level singletons
94. /// (`frame::INSTANCE`/`INSTANCE_INIT` and the `PhysMemoryManager`/`Upool` singletons)
95. /// whose value is not directly spec-readable. The cross-call transition (`v -> v'`) is
96. /// realized in the proving phase by a ghost token over those singletons (see
97. /// `view_design.md` section 8); during the specification phase it is read like `self@`.
98. pub uninterp spec fn phys_view() -> PhysModView;
99. 
100. impl PhysModView {
101.     /// Well-formedness invariant of the subsystem.
102.     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
103.         // Once the allocator is up, the frame partition is well formed.
104.         &&& self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
105.         // The manager layer can only be up if the allocator is up.
106.         &&& self.manager_ready ==> self.initialized
107.     }
108. 
109.     /// The subsystem is fully brought up and self-consistent.
110.     pub open spec fn live(self) -> bool {
111.         &&& self.initialized
112.         &&& self.manager_ready
113.         &&& self.frames.wf()
114.     }
115. }
116. 
117. //==================================================================================================
118. // Frame-set vocabulary (on the existing FrameAllocView)
119. //==================================================================================================
120. 
121. impl FrameAllocView {
122.     /// The allocator tracks (covers) the frame at `addr` — it is one of the frames this
123.     /// allocator knows about, allocated or free. Models `frame::is_covered`.
124.     pub open spec fn covers(self, addr: int) -> bool {
125.         self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) || self.free_frames.contains(addr)
126.     }
127. 
128.     /// The frame at `addr` is reserved: present in the allocated set, hence `alloc()` can
129.     /// never return it. This is the core caller-visible fact a "booked" frame satisfies.
130.     pub open spec fn reserved(self, addr: int) -> bool {
131.         self.allocated_frames.contains(addr)
132.     }
133. 
134.     /// Every frame address in `set` is reserved.
135.     pub open spec fn all_reserved(self, set: Set<int>) -> bool {
136.         forall|a: int| set.contains(a) ==> self.reserved(a)
137.     }
138. 
139.     /// Every frame address in `set` is currently free (booking precondition: a range can be
140.     /// booked only if it is entirely free).
141.     pub open spec fn all_free(self, set: Set<int>) -> bool {
142.         forall|a: int| #[trigger] set.contains(a) ==> self.free_frames.contains(a)
143.     }
144. 
145.     /// Reserve every frame in `set` (each assumed free in `self`): move it from
146.     /// `free_frames` to `allocated_frames` with refcount 1.
147.     pub open spec fn book_all(self, set: Set<int>) -> FrameAllocView {
148.         FrameAllocView {
149.             allocated_frames: self.allocated_frames.union(set),
150.             free_frames: self.free_frames.difference(set),
151.             refcounts: self.refcounts.union_prefer_right(
152.                 Map::new(|a: int| set.contains(a), |a: int| 1int),
153.             ),
154.         }
155.     }
156. 
157.     /// Reserve only the *covered* frames of `set`; skip the rest (coverage-gated). Models
158.     /// the MMIO booking rule.
159.     pub open spec fn book_covered(self, set: Set<int>) -> FrameAllocView {
160.         self.book_all(set.filter(|a: int| self.covers(a)))
161.     }
162. }
163. 
164. /// Page-aligned physical frame addresses covered by a region `[start, start + size)`.
165. /// Mirrors the frame-set computation used by `frame::alloc_range`.
166. pub open spec fn region_frame_addrs(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
167.     let start_frame_number = start / spec_page_size();
168.     let end_frame_number = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
169.     vstd::set_lib::set_int_range(start_frame_number, end_frame_number)
170.         .map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
171. }
172. 
173. /// The set of physical frame addresses covered by all regions in a physical
174. /// non-usable-memory list. Uninterpreted: `LinkedList` has no Verus model, so its contents
175. /// cannot be folded over in spec; this names the abstract union of `region_frame_addrs`
176. /// over the list, which is all the contract needs.
177. pub uninterp spec fn phys_regions_frame_set(
178.     regions: &::alloc::collections::LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>>,
179. ) -> Set<int>;
180. 
181. /// The set of physical frame addresses covered by all MMIO regions in a list (after
182. /// GVA->GPA translation). Uninterpreted for the same reason as `phys_regions_frame_set`.
183. pub uninterp spec fn mmio_regions_frame_set(
184.     regions: &::alloc::collections::LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<VirtualAddress>>,
185. ) -> Set<int>;
186. 
187. } // end verus!

4. //! Frame allocator — module-level singleton.
5. //!
6. //! The frame allocator is backed by a [`Bitmap`] and exposed as free functions over a
7. //! singleton so every in-kernel caller goes through the same state. No struct-valued handle is
8. //! passed around.
9. //!
10. //! Access to the frame allocator is synchronized externally and performed by a single thread, so
11. //! the backing bitmap uses non-atomic operations.
12. 
13. //==================================================================================================
14. // Imports
15. //==================================================================================================
16.

18.     mem::{
19.         FrameAddress,
20.         PageAligned,
21.         PhysicalAddress,
22.         TruncatedMemoryRegion,
23.     },
24.     platform::NFRAMES,
25. };
